title: Beef Burrito
subtitle: Spiced beef, rice, and beans wrapped in a large flour tortilla
excerpt: A substantial Tex-Mex burrito: spiced beef mince layered with Mexican-style rice, seasoned black beans, soured cream, and cheese, all wrapped tightly in a large flour tortilla. Filling enough to be the whole meal.
sourceNotes: Beef burritos: a Tex-Mex staple. The Mission burrito style (large flour tortilla, multiple fillings layered) developed in San Francisco in the 1960s; the simpler two-filling version is a Tex-Mex home-kitchen standard. Based on classic American Tex-Mex cooking sources.

recipe.freezeNotes: Wrap assembled burritos individually in foil and freeze for up to 3 months. Reheat in the oven at 180°C for 20-25 minutes from frozen.
recipe.batchNotes: Double the beef and rice filling and freeze the assembled burritos for future meals.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The beef filling and rice can be made a day ahead and reheated.

glossaryTerms.definition: A large flour tortilla wrapped tightly around a filling of meat, rice, beans, cheese, and/or vegetables. The name means 'little donkey' in Spanish, though the origin of the connection is disputed.

content.text: is a large flour tortilla wrapped tightly around spiced beef, rice, beans, and cheese. The wrap holds everything in one portable bundle. The beef cooks in 15 minutes; the rice takes 20. The layering order matters: rice at the base (it's the heaviest), then beef, then beans, then cheese and soured cream on top so they don't make the wrap soggy.
Large flour tortillas work best here; a standard medium wrap won't hold the full filling without splitting. Warm them before folding so they stay pliable.

Put {{long-grain-rice}} of rice in a saucepan with {{stock-chicken}} of stock and the cumin. Bring to a boil, reduce to the lowest heat, cover, and cook for 12 minutes. Remove from the heat and leave to steam, covered, for 5 minutes.

Heat {{vegetable-oil}} of oil in a frying pan. Cook {{onion}} finely chopped onion for 5 minutes. Add {{garlic}} of crushed garlic for 1 minute. Add {{beef-mince}} of beef mince; cook 5-6 minutes until browned. Stir in the chilli powder, cumin, smoked paprika, and {{tomato-puree}} of tomato purée. Cook 2 minutes. Season with salt.
Warm the drained black beans in a small pan with the cumin and a pinch of salt. They just need to be warm; no need to mash them.
Warm each flour tortilla in a dry pan for 30 seconds on each side.
Layer the fillings on the lower third of the tortilla: rice first, then beef, then beans, then cheese, soured cream, avocado and coriander. Don't overfill; leave 4-5 cm free at the bottom and sides.
Fold the bottom edge up over the filling. Fold the sides in tightly. Roll up from the bottom, pressing the filling in as you go. Eat immediately or wrap in foil to hold its shape.

items.fix: Warm the tortilla first so it's pliable. Use a moderate amount of filling; too much makes rolling impossible. The fold-sides-first technique keeps everything in.

items.symptom: Burrito is soggy at the base
items.cause: Wet fillings placed directly onto the tortilla
items.fix: Put rice at the base (it absorbs moisture) and keep the soured cream near the top. Drain beans well before adding.

items.symptom: Rice is undercooked in the centre
items.cause: Lid lifted during the steaming step
items.fix: Do not lift the lid during the 5-minute steam off the heat; the residual steam finishes the cooking. Lifting the lid lets the steam escape.

items.symptom: Filling is too sparse across the whole burrito
items.cause: Filling spread too thin across the whole tortilla
items.fix: Pile the filling on the lower third of the tortilla only; spread to the sides but not right to the edge. Rolling from the bottom brings the filling through the whole wrap.

content.text: The flour tortilla burrito is a product of northern Mexico and the US Southwest, where wheat flour (rather than corn) became the tortilla of choice due to the climate. The multi-filling version common in the US today was developed in San Francisco's Mission district in the 1960s. It's now one of the most widely made Tex-Mex dishes in home kitchens on both sides of the Atlantic.
